utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody in the courtroom. Before the witness is being brought in, the Chamber would like to raise two matters. The first is related to a problem we have dealt with last week already. That was the issue concerning the tendering of unofficial and uncorrected transcripts by the Prosecution. This matter was raised by the Chamber during the proceedings on Monday, the 26th of April. The Chamber has recently been informed that the Registry had -- in fact, all the transcripts tendered so far during the trial sessions are, in fact, unofficial and uncorrected. Therefore, the Chamber would like to ask you, Mr. Tolimir, whether you have any submissions in this regard before the Chamber is inclined to deal with it further.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I'd like to greet everybody present and all those following the trial. May there be peace among us, and with God's will let these proceedings pass smoothly. Now, Mr. President, just those who -- the ones that are corrected, not the ones that somebody is going to brush up. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In fact, I didn't understand your position, Mr. Tolimir. Do you have any submissions with regard to receiving of transcripts of previous trials with some witnesses we are hearing here, the corrected or the uncorrected and unofficial versions? The previous versions were all uncorrected and unofficial, and, therefore, the Chamber addressed this problem to the Prosecution to replace them by the official and corrected versions. Do you have any comments to that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. When I said "corrected," I meant those that have been verified and corrected and looked through officially, not those with mistakes that have not been verified. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The Chamber, by this oral decision, instructs the Prosecution to replace the unofficial and uncorrected transcripts that have been admitted so far with the official and corrected versions. These concerned Exhibits P29, P36, P37, P49, P60, P69, P97, P98, and P102. The other matter the Chamber would like to raise is the following: The Chamber has received an e-mail from the Defence, dated 27th of April, whereby the Defence seeks admission of a number of exhibits used with Witness 53, that is, PW-015, during the cross-examination on the 26th of April. The Chamber notes, firstly, that two of the exhibits mentioned in the e-mail have, in fact, already been admitted into evidence as D26 and D27. These are the 65 ter numbers 1D47 and 1D48 on the list attached to this e-mail by the Defence. Secondly, the Chamber notes that seeking admission of exhibits used with the witnesses in court by way of an e-mail, after the witness's evidence has already concluded, is not the appropriate course of action. The Defence had ample opportunity to seek admission of these exhibits in the course of cross-examination on the 26th of April. This would have provided the Prosecution the opportunity to raise objections, if any, to the admission of these exhibits. As this is the first instance where the Chamber has received a request of this nature from the Defence by way of an e-mail, the Chamber proposes to do the following: Provided that the Prosecution does not have objections to the admission of the exhibits listed in the e-mail, all of which were used extensively with the Witness PW-015, the Chamber is inclined to admit into evidence the exhibits listed in the Defence e-mail which are not already in evidence. This concerns the 65 ter numbers 1D81, 1D82, 1D50, and 1D52. Mr. McCloskey, is the Prosecution in a position to state whether it has objections to the admission of these exhibits?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours. If I could have one second. Mr. President, the Prosecution has no objection to what are noted as images 50 and 52. However, 81 and 82 are witness statements, and unless there's some special reason for a witness statement to come in in its entirety, I think it was used fairly on cross-examination, but unless there's something special or a special reason, we would object to the statements coming in in their entirety. Otherwise, witnesses will be followed by their statements, and there's many, many statements. Anything that's used in cross-examination, I don't think, is, by itself, a reason for a statement to come in, unless, of course, the Chamber wishes to see all these statements, which some Trial Chambers do, and that's fine. But it was not my understanding that you wanted to see all the witness statements. And, of course, the relevant portions were read to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. McCloskey. First of all, the Chamber will receive the photographs, 65 ter 1D50 and 65 ter 1D52, as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter 1D50 will be Exhibit D29. 65 ter 1D52 will be Exhibit D30, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Taking into account your objection to the other two documents, the Chamber will consider the matter further during the next break, and we'll inform the parties on its decision later. The witness should be brought in. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, 81 and 82, you don't have to admit into evidence, and that's not something we requested either. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I'm surprised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: If I understood the e-mail by the Defence correctly, that you were tendering them by e-mail. We will deal with that later. Thank you. Good afternoon, Mr. Ruez.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Welcome back to the Tribunal for continuing the cross-examination. First of all, I would like to remind you that the affirmation you made at the beginning of your examination still applies.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please sit down. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Let me introduce myself. My name is Aleksandar Gajic. I am legal assistant for Zdravko Tolimir. I'd like to raise an administrative issue. The Court Officer was sent an e-mail linked to certain problems linked to e-court and not for the documents, part 81 and 82, to be admitted into evidence. Namely, the problem was with the photographs that were admitted into evidence, but were not within the system the following day. So that was the problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. As I indicated just now, we will deal with that later and check that. Mr. Tolimir, you are now in the position to continue your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone for the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You need the microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Ruez, good afternoon, and welcome. I'd like to remind you of this. On page 16268, lines 18 and 20 of the transcript, you said: "The object of the investigation was not to establish how many people managed to live and leave the security zone of Srebrenica, but to determine the destiny of those who were proclaimed missing." Are those your words?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, these are my words, and I confirm what I previously said.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, at the end of your cross-examination, and I'd like to remind you of this because of continuity, you said -- 10766 page, lines 12 to 25, and 1077 [as interpreted], lines 1 and 2 of the transcript you said, and I quote: "Already in July or August 1995, while we were in Tuzla, during the summer, we had access to several hundred statements from the Commission for War Crimes, and as I've already said, from the Ministry of the Interior as well -- similarly, from the United Nations Sector for Civilian Affairs. We also handed out questionnaires to the refugees camps and non-government organisations so as to --" or, rather, "which would have anything with any relevant information, to contact us. Now, on the basis of that, we drew up several packages, if I could put it that way. One package of measures were those -- were people who had information. The second group were people who had something important to tell us about the deportation route from Potocari to Kladanj, and the main statements, those that were most important, were from the last group, which claimed that the witnesses either saw the killings or were executed." So I think that's what we were discussing the last time. Did I quote you correctly? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. We have rough packages in which we separated potential witnesses. It could be more detailed, but this was, indeed, the situation at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ruez, my next question is this, the first question: Did you look at the reasons for which Srebrenica -- people left Srebrenica, because you referred to deportation here, so did you look into the reasons, and the Defence talks about the Muslims leaving Srebrenica? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not really up to me, I think, to answer the question, because the transport of a population, for me, it's, let's say, the people, as you say, who evacuated the enclave. But when there can be some legal considerations to look into, this is not part of my work, but the work of Prosecution to determine if this transfer of population is a foreseeable transfer or deportation whatsoever. So I confirm, indeed, we looked into the aspect of the evacuation of a population who was inside the enclave. Now, you also asked me, I think, if we looked into the reason why these people left. The conclusion of the investigation, as you most certainly know, is that in Potocari the behaviour of the Bosnian Army was designed to inflict such terror to these people that they would leave on their own will this area. That was planned by those who decided to take it over at that time, and this is the reason why these people voluntarily tried to get on board of the buses before being separated by this squadron of Bosnian Serb soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ruez. Thank you. Now, my second question is this: Did you, as an investigator, deal with the question of who took the decision to leave Srebrenica? Thank you. May I ask for shorter answers adjusted to the question I asked, please.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: To make it, in that case, very short: As far as I know, the decision to leave was made individually by all those who had the feeling that had they not left, they would have been captured and subsequently killed. This is the main reason why these people left.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ruez. My question was: Did you investigate it or not? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not a precise point of investigation, but any witness with whom myself or other investigators took interviews from raised this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ruez. Now, my next question is this: In categorising the witnesses, when you categorise them - you mentioned that on the 30th of March and I read through it a moment ago - you mentioned a number of categories of witnesses, but no mention is made of witnesses about the events in the column. Did you interview witnesses like that, too, and did you attach importance to them in order to determine the destiny of those who were proclaimed missing? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely, for the main reason that among those who ended up prisoners under the control of the Bosnian Serb Army, you have two main groups. The group 1 is those who got separated when trying to get on board of buses during the evacuation of the Srebrenica enclave, and the second much larger group is those who were among this column who had been trapped between Srebrenica and Konjevic Polje, and when adopting a massive surrender process at the 13, in the morning, it is among this group that you find the most future survivors of the executions that were done the two following days -- on the three, four following day in the area north.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ruez. Perhaps you didn't understand me properly. What I meant was those who were in the column and left and went to Tuzla, that is to say, those who passed through the line and the route from Srebrenica to Baljkovica to Tuzla. So my question would be the following: Did you have an occasion to receive statements from the Bosnian authorities about this category of persons, those who managed to break through and left, and did they give statements of that kind to the police and the army, and did you have any special instructions for taking statements from people who transferred from Srebrenica to BH territory? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand the question, General. Yes, it is a group in which we initially looked into. The goal was not to reconstruct the military adventure between Konjevic Polje and Nezuk, but to find out if in that military action in process there had also been some crimes that would have to be dealt with by this investigation. The reality is the few people we wished to interview were put up front by the BiH Army. They had very little to say. At least they had nothing to say about any kind of atrocity during this military operation, which was battle. And since it was battle, it was very quickly taken out of our screen of what was the main purpose of the investigation, which was to find out what happened to the missing people.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ruez. Since you're talking about the destiny of those who went missing, and those left in Nezuk, in the column, they knew about a large number of people who disappeared, the whole front of the column. That's why I'm interested in whether you had statements of that kind at all. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the total amount of this column that left Srebrenica on the evening of the 11 and the 12, we already talked about it, with an estimate with around 15.000, what is official from the BiH side is that 6.000 members of the 28th Division managed to cross the lines in the area of Nezuk, so indeed there will always be a question mark about those who, in that process, missed -- in combat missed by crossing the lines in minefields or in any other combat operation. This is the reason why the -- I already talked about this. The only number the criminal investigation takes into account is the number of people who have been found in the primary mass graves that we connect with execution sites and regroupment [sic] points, and later on scientifically connect with those found in the secondary graves and who are coming from these primary graves. And this is the only number that the criminal investigation takes into account, because this is the number of those we can prove have been under the control of those who had taken them prisoners, the Bosnian Serb Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ruez. We'll come back to that later on, but let's go back to my next question, whether in the graves there were those who were killed in battle and those who were killed otherwise. We'll come back to that. But this is my question: May we have 1D63 displayed on our screens, please? It's a document from the army, BH Army, the Command of the 2nd Corps, the Security Department, confidential 06101-160-8/95 of the 10th of August, 1995, and it refers to the assignments. We still haven't got it up on our screens. May we have it called up on e-court, please. It's come up on our screens in Serbian, but not in English. And since I don't have the translation, I'm going to quote: "The statements you sent us --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It always takes a certain time that these are brought up on the screen. Just be a little bit more patient. You must not quote everything. It's not necessary. We have it now on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: "The statements you sent us," that's what it says in this document, "attached to the above reference letter contain information relating, for the most part, to the transit of the group of combatants and civilians to from Srebrenica to the free territory, and very few or no facts at all about war crimes and the crime of genocide. According to the guide-lines we have given you, as well as the instructions you received during the lecture delivered on the 3rd of August, 1995, at the Veterans Centre of the 2nd Corps Command, you should have taken statements on the circumstances surrounding the war crimes and crime of genocide." And that's the end of my quotation from the document. But he goes on to say: "In the handouts you received," that is to say, at the lectures, "contain detailed and easily understandable descriptions of what a statement relating to these specific circumstances should contain, starting from personal details of the interviewee, to other intrinsic and essential elements. The statements you supplied do not follow these rules." In this statement, it goes on to say: "Act in the following sense and carry out the instructions issued." Now, my question to you is this: When you looked at the statements, were you aware that there was special requirements for those taking statements from the interviewees and the elements that each statement must contain, having to do with the circumstances of war crimes and crimes against humanity? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand very well the point. Be certain of one thing. The only statements that we've ended up taking into consideration are statements of people who were interviewed by ICTY personnel, not by BiH Army, BiH police, or BiH War Crime Commission. These statements were the basis of identification of persons who we would have an interest to talk with. And, indeed, the way these statements were taken probably needed some improvement by those who conducted the interview, since they were very short and didn't necessarily enter into details. The reason why: These people were systematically re-interviewed by ICTY personnel, and the information inside the statements was then later the topic of a focus of the following steps of investigation. That was to identify the places where they reported events and analyse these spots in order to confirm or infirm the credibility of these witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ruez. Now I have to put another question that will contain your answer to the first question, because you gave a rather lengthy answer. Since you had certain contacts with representatives of the 28th Division, are you aware that on the 3rd of August, 1995, they held this lecture where they issued the instructions on the way to collect information from members of the 28th Division? In other words, do you know of this, and do you know that there were special instructions given to these people? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had extremely little contact with members of the 28th Division, since, as I told you, we probably interviewed two soldiers who made the spear-head and arrived in Tuzla. For the rest, I didn't know anything about whatever instructions could be given by the 2nd Corps to its members in August. No, I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ruez. Tell me, please, as you were in a position to review a large number of statements, almost all of them, as you said, and you even interviewed some of the Muslims who managed to pull out, in this document it says: "The statements provided do not contain or contain very few facts related to war crimes and the crime of genocide." My question is this: Are you sure that you actually reviewed a large number of such statements, and can you recall the date of these statements referring to the executions? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No short answer possible on this. The first point: What is in this letter is a reality, since those who were at the spear-head of a column could not witness any war crime because they were in the battle situation, all these crimes happened in their back, to those who were left behind. So -- but first fact. When -- the second part of your question, please remind me. There was something else.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: When did you observe that statements do contain information about executions, and up until when were there statements when no such information appeared? I am referring to the time-frame. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection to compound questions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sorry. The compound questions are very difficult for even a witness of this calibre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, could you please always wait until you get the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Now you may make your comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection to the compound nature of the question. It's very difficult to pick out the different questions, even for a witness as experienced as Mr. Ruez. If we could not put multi-questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, I think this witness is capable to deal with difficult questions as well. And if there are any problems, you should raise them in cross-examination. Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay, I understand your question, General. Most of the statements we had access to, this was during the period between 20 July, the date of the arrival of our tiny little team in the Tuzla area, so interview process started some three or four days later. And we continued this process until, more or less, the 20th of August. In that time-frame, the police and the War Crime Commission were continuing to take statements, so the main phase was to quickly run through these, indeed, hundreds of pieces of information and extract from them those that we intended to interview as priority witnesses, in order then later, but this was in September, take all this information and try to draw a story through time, what I call the first criminal analysis of the situation. So most of the key witnesses, indeed - I'm talking about the survivors - were identified and interviewed during that summer, at the exception of one of them, who was one of the survivors of the Kravica warehouse, who could only be interviewed, if I recall well, in April 1996 because he was among one of the last groups, part of a prisoner exchange that happened, I think, in February or March 1996. And I understand also, but this happened after I had left the Tribunal in 2001, that one additional survivor for the Orahovac site had been identified much later, and as far as I know he testified in this courtroom a few days ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. McCloskey [as interpreted]. I would like to say this: The document that I have read out from that you have before you on the screens was produced on the 10th of August, and you say that you have completed your interviews by the 28th of August. Does that mean that all the statements that you consider relevant were actually compiled between the 20th of July, up until the 28th of August, as stated here, or did you obtain them later on from BH organs? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, again I have to insist that the only information we got from BiH authorities were the primary information that they could collect, but our only source -- real source of information, which then we used in order to orientate the investigation on the material aspect, that is, finding crime scenes, is based on the interviews that we took -- we, ICTY investigators, took during that summer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ruez. Does that relate to the period between the 20th of July and the 20th of August? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This was, in fact, the first round of interviews that we took, because this interview process lasted during the six years I was at the head of this investigation. In terms of victims, it lasted until at least the end of 1997, since each time we could come across useful information, we investigated this information if it was worth the effort, and after that the interview process slipped more on to interviewing BiH police and military personnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ruez. As I've said, this document was produced on the 10th of August, 1995. And judging by the statements that we have received, I see that the statements -- only the statements written after that time, the word "war crimes" and "genocide" is mentioned that was contained in the statement. Was it commonplace for individuals who are not educated and who do not have any experience with international criminal law to use such terms, because they always indicate whether some act was a war crime or a crime of genocide? Thank you. If the question is not clear, I can repeat it.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's clear. I mean, what is clear to me is that this document is probably written by the legal officer of the 2nd Corps, so this man has some notions of legal qualifications, so war crimes, genocide, things like this. I did not see this type of rhetoric in the statements of those that we have personally interviewed, though at that time genocide was a quite common notion, since everyone was throwing it in the face of the other one that genocide had been committed against him. So it was a very common rhetoric even at that time, and it had become even worse in the years following the end of this conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ruez. We have heard evidence and have seen statements from that period, and we see that from the 10th of August, the word "genocide" is used by the individuals who provided the statements. If necessary, I will show it to the -- I will point it out to the Trial Chamber, based on the statements that we've heard and evidence that we've heard from witnesses who appeared so far. Now, tell us, please, what are the -- we see that various organs of the BH government sought this information. What are those organs? Could you tell us, please?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I have to insist that the only investigation and the only witness statements we have relied on were those of people we have interviewed ourselves, meaning members of the Office of the Prosecutor. And to repeat again, the providers of witness statements that we used in order to fine-tune who would be the most interesting ones, they were two main sort of information; BiH police and mostly the War Crime Commission. We had a few -- a handful of statements of BiH soldiers, a handful, and who had nothing to report because they were at the head of a column that went through Nezuk. So since they never ended up prisoner, they had nothing to say about any war crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ruez. My question related to the time-frame and the pace at which you received these. And you said that you did not receive them for the security organs, but rather from the MUP and the commission, but here we can see that the security organs were the ones who actually determined how this whole process was going to go on.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is your conclusion, General. I cannot comment this. Again, the 2nd Corps was not our point of contact at that time. The first contact with them was at least two and a half years after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ruez. You've stated here that 6.000 fighters managed to cross over from Srebrenica to Tuzla, and probably that was a significant pool from which you tried to obtain information, which would mean that the security organs had to assist in that work because that was the largest number of people that you referred to that you interviewed, or do you also refer to the ones who did not actually manage to break through? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, the first part of your statement is totally incorrect. This was not the main pool of information. This was the most microscopic pool of information, since, I repeat, those who have managed to went through the lines are those who have nothing to say to people investigating the fate of the missing. The military operation -- the small military operation part of this case is, again, not the focus of investigation and these people who are not, far from it, among the interesting witnesses for this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ruez. We've seen a video here shown by Mr. McCloskey when he said that you would actually comment on the video, and on it we could see a fighter who had managed to break through and who said that he had run into four different ambushes. And how is it that there is no mention of that here, since you say that there were 3.000 individuals involved?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the accused please repeat the last part of his question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, again, reconstructing the military history of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Ruez, could you please pause a moment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The last part of the question was not interpreted properly. Mr. Tolimir, could you please repeat the last part of your question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I will try to reconstruct my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So we've seen a video here --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, only the last part, only the last part.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: -- showing a soldier, who said that he had run into four ambushes, and that there were 3.000 killed. Were you interested in the number of missing persons, because these 3.000 would be missing people? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. Again, I repeat that the military history of what happened between -- during the breakthrough of an armed part of a column is not the goal of the investigation, of the criminal investigation. But, indeed, this soldier is certainly right. They went through several ambushes, military operations, not in the frame of investigation, and that, indeed, I concede that among the 8.000 missing people, those who will not be found in the graves will be considered as missing in action. So, again, I attract your attention on the number of those who are found inside the graves, who are identified by DNA, and subtracting this final number to the total number of missing people registered in the ICRC book, will give you an approximate of those who have to be considered missing in action.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ruez. Was the purpose of the investigation to determine what happened with these 3.000 men who were killed in ambushes? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The assessment of this soldier on tape saying it's 3.000 people killed is more or less to be taken with the same caution than when the Bosnian Serb soldier, at the bottom of a hill, says that they captured 5.000 on that spot that day. It's impossible to know if these people have a real precise assessment of these numbers. This is why, again, I will repeat it probably every half an hour during two days, the important number in this case is the people who have been found in the mass graves and that we can prove they have gone through a cold-blooded execution process, organised and systematic. And at this point, if my information is correct, I think we arrive at something like 6.400.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Ruez, my question is: Was it in the interest of the investigation to determine what happened with the bodies of those who had been killed in ambushes? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The places we have found and in which the victims have been found buried are locations very nearby concentration spots of prisoners, and we also know from the engineer records the pace at which these people have been buried. So if you look more in detail the situation, you could imply that in these mass graves, we have found, in fact, people who have been killed in action. In that case, indeed, the events at Nezuk, ongoing combat or little time of no combat, doesn't make it credible that these people are in the graves we have opened.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ruez. Tell us, please, where, then, were those people who were killed in ambush, in combat, on minefields, where were they buried? They were not buried in the territory of the BH Army, not in Republika Srpska, you say they were not found in the mass graves. Tell us and tell this Court, where are they? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: You say that the graves are not in the Republika Srpska. I cannot confirm that. Either they have left -- been left on the surface, and this the Commission for Missing People and Exhumation of Bosniak Government could probably give some answers on this. But the fact is that finding graves whereof cleaning of the terrain has taken in the place following the 16 of July, has not been, indeed, a point of research for this case. We were focusing finding mass graves with victims of execution, not with victims of combat operations. And I will also have to add that all questions regarding the detailed findings inside the graves, I won't be the relevant person to be asked about this, since there are two other experts who testify about the mass grave findings; Professor Richard Wright for all what is the pathology aspects and also my colleague Dean Manning for all what is the results of police labs on the findings.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ruez. I read out a portion where you talked about the missing persons, and now all of a sudden you are not interested in the missing persons unless they were in mass graves or murdered in some kind of mass crime. In the same way, this statement of the security organs only focus on war crimes and crime of genocide. They do not try to establish the people who were killed in combat operations. So now tell us, please, how is this Court and how are we to determine what happened with the bodies of those who were killed in action? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's the responsibility of every government to try to find the bodies of his own soldiers killed in any military operation, but I can confirm that it is not the purpose and not the goal of a criminal investigation team to try to identify people who are missing in action. Our goal is to try to find out if victims say the truth, reconstruct a chronology of events, prove what has happened, and try to identify the perpetrators to bring them to a courtroom, not identifying missing soldiers killed in action.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ruez. You say that as an investigator. Security organs also say that they're only interested in war crimes and genocide. Does that mean that nobody actually investigated how those who went missing in action were killed and that the large number of them actually were killed there, rather than what you're doing, placing them in mass graves in large numbers? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not a question for me, General. It's a question for the BiH authorities, who try to find out the fate of their own missing soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ruez. It's not a question for you; right. Now, would this be a question for you: Along with the communication route, in your statement you say from Konjevic Polje part of the people were killed not in fighting and not in executions. So you don't know where to put them, which group. Where did you find them, in mass graves, and which number -- which group did you assigned them to, and how many of them were there? If you can tell me that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It might be a little bug in the translation, because I read that it had said that at Konjevic Polje, part of the people were killed not in fighting and not in execution. I don't understand. It's either one or the other one. If not, it's a natural cause of death. There might be a little translation problem, I would believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Ruez, it's not a problem of the translation. The problem is that in the interview that you gave to "The Monitor," you said that you don't know where to place part of the people who were neither executed, nor, in your opinion, were killed in battle; how to classify them, you didn't know. Can you explain where we can classify them, then? And it's document 1D60, so may we have called up 1D60.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm just going to object. May the witness be allowed -- when something that specific is referred to, if the witness could have a chance to look at -- and I think he's caught that, so I think I can withdraw my objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. May we have page 25 displayed, please, from "The Monitor," and I'm going to quote part of the statement, as requested by the Prosecution. Thank you. We see the statement on our screens. It was given to "The Monitor," and the Prosecutor disclosed it to us. And in the second column, paragraph 2, it says, and I quote --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, may I ask you, is there an English translation? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We submitted this for translation a long time ago. It's with the Interpretation Service, but we haven't received the translation of it yet. So I don't know. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In that case, you should read out the relevant portion, but please indicate very precisely which part you are reading.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I'm reading the portion of the text marked on page 0603-8344, lines 2 -- or, rather, the second column, second paragraph, and I'm going to quote that and read it out: "There is a specific feature. One of the graves in Glogova contains the bodies of people who were killed along the road from Konjevic Polje to Kravica. The Serbs will say that they were killed in battle, whereas, in fact, they were killed as soon as they set foot on the asphalt road. This was not a combat situation, and neither were they prisoners. Quite simply, they killed them as soon as they set foot on the road, and we're going to add them to the find number."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Now, my question to you is this: Since these people were buried in the Glogova grave, how many of them are there? Thank you?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Glogova is the most difficult crime scene in terms of mass graves because, indeed, the persons buried at Glogova have three origins. One origin of them is the burial spot of most of those who have been killed in Kravica. I say "most" because initially the first truck-loads were taken to a little hill nearby and dumped alongside the edge of this hill. So most of the people killed in Kravica were shifted towards Glogova. Unfortunately, also at Glogova were buried bodies of those who were killed once they had reached the asphalt road, an unknown number of people. And the third origin, unfortunately, is also those who have been killed in Bratunac town. So there is a mixture of origins of bodies in this grave that make it, for example, in the future impossible to know very precisely how many people have been killed in Kravica, because the transfer of the bodies of Glogova we know is south of Srebrenica, but even once all the exhumations would have been finalised, it would not be able to provide the number of those killed in Kravica because of these various origin of bodies that cannot be separated each from another.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ruez. And did you count them -- or, rather, did you add them to the number and include them in the number of those who were killed?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, all those who have been found at Glogova were included in the final number, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And for their killing, is it those who should be -- who stand accused here or those who actually killed them? Who should be held responsible? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you know, General, the only people siting in this courtroom are those who are considered the utmost responsible. The other ones, they have to be sent to the State Court in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I just asked you: Who should be tried for their death, those who are accused of having conducting the execution or those who took part in battle pursuant to commands from their superior commander?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, this is not an appropriate question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's a question of command responsibility. I'm not tasked to deal with command responsibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Carry on, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, since the witness does not want to give us the number of those killed or who died, whereas I am being accused of those killings, and that's why I am asking what the number of those killed was and who should be held responsible for those killings. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think you know very well that at the end of the day, this Chamber will consider that question, and not the witness. The witness may answer your questions about the number of missing or killed people, but not the personal responsibility. This is not a question to deal with during the cross-examination. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. And thank you, Mr. Ruez. I'm not holding it against you. I am grateful to you and thanking you, and I'm not angry because you put forward this dilemma, because it is really -- it really is a dilemma. So thank you for raising it. And I would like to ask you a question which is of vital interest to the Defence. For example, in the Krstic trial, in your testimony you put forward a number of interesting pieces of information which were not presented here by the Prosecution at this particular trial, and the Defence considers that they are of great importance to establishing the relevant facts in this trial. Now may we have 1D100 called up, please, and shown to the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, to avoid further problems, are you tendering this document, the interview in "The Monitor," as an exhibit?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President, we are tendering this document into evidence, and we shall be discussing it further. I just asked a question linked to the problem that we're discussing now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection to this coming in. It looks like it's a question-and-answer -- it looks like a statement and should not -- I'm not aware of any rules that allow such a statement or even a newspaper article to come in as evidence. He's used -- the party's used that, and that is part of the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This interview in "The Monitor" without English translation will be marked for identification so that if it will be used during this cross-examination or with other witnesses, we know what was it about. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Ms. Stewart was able to find an English version of that and has sent it to the Defence. So if it's necessary, we can get it up on the screen again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I appreciate that. Just a moment. We would like to have the English version on the screen. We have this "Monitor" article on the screen in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Ms. Stewart reminded me that I was being a bit optimistic. It's got to get in the e-court system. Apparently she pulled it off our system. And we can get one down here very quickly and get it on the old-fashioned ELMO, but it will be just a few minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. McCloskey, then the Chamber will mark that for identification, pending translation, and then we will deal with that later.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That would be Exhibit D31, marked for identification, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. In the meantime, we have another document on the screen. Please carry on, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I'd like the statement that was on e-court, 1D63, to be tendered into evidence, please. Thank you. I mean the statement given by the security organs that I quoted from earlier on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes. We were very busy with "The Monitor" interview, we didn't realise that you had put any question to this witness related to this transcript on the screen. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think he's asked for the BiH document into evidence, and we have no objection to that, if that's what he was talking about, the document that wanted a little more detail in the reports of the people coming through the column. And Ms. Stewart's figured out a way to show us the English version of "Monitor" as well, if that is needed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Any further comment, Mr. Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I've already asked for the next document, the one from the Krstic trial, and it is 1D100. May that be called up, please, several pages from the Krstic trial related to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you are ahead of the proceedings. The statement of the transcript we have on the screen at the moment, you have tendered that, and the Chamber will receive it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think we have figured out the situation. The document we saw first was the document of the 10th of August, 1995, Command of the 2nd Corps of the BH Army. That will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be D32, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We have before us 1D100. It is the transcript from the Krstic trial, relating to the events and investigation linked to Bare and Kamenica, those two places. Now, first, on page 589, you say the following: "I would also like to mark the village of Bare which many people have been pointing to who had knowledge of the area, know a little bit where they were going, and not only following the person in front of them."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Now, my question to you is this. I quoted what you said, and now here is my question: Can you, on the one of the previous maps, draw in the village of Bare, the location of the village of Bare? And perhaps the best map would be the map on page 23 of your book, which is 65 ter 01450, page 23. It's a Prosecution exhibit. Thank you. Thank you. Here we have the map on our screens. It's 65 ter 01450, a Prosecution exhibit, and the page is 23. Mr. Ruez, would you please mark the position of Bare, the Bare locality?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: To point precisely, Bare, as understand on such map, would be difficult. But, nevertheless, as we said, area of regroupment [sic] was the area of [indiscernible] Jaglici, then the escape route was going, let's say, roughly north in the direction of Kravica, and behind the hills in the area of Kravica is the area of Bare and Kamenica. And, indeed, these are locations where ambushes took place, at 12.00 in the evening -- afternoon/evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ruez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Would you mark that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You want me to mark it? Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: As accurately as possible.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Roughly, the escape route [marks]. And the area we are talking about would be somewhere in this area here [marks].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You mean by that the location of Bare?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's the rough area that I circled, Bare/Kamenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ruez. Would you mark in Bare again and put "B" or "Bare." Write in "Bare" or the letter B on this map, too, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before we go on, are you tendering for marking the first one? It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit D33, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Will that include the marking by Mr. Ruez of the place and the route?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The original map was already received. The map with the markings is now an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. It didn't say "Bare" on it, but the transcript explains it all.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Now, on page 589, lines 22 and 23, and I'm referring to the transcript from the Krstic trial - may we go back to that, please - you state, and I quote, these are your words: "Bare was also a place where there were ambushes and where there was shelling. Many people were wounded on this territory." My question to you now is this: Can you tell us, roughly speaking, how many witnesses linked to the -- that were linked to the event around Bare village? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could not answer precisely, because this is part of reconstruction to understand the chronology of events. But since it is ambush/shelling on a column with mixed civilian and military, it is considered by the investigation as a military operation. This is why there was no specific focus assigned this one, but the situation it generated is still interesting for the continuity of what happened after that because it is these ambushes that also demoralised the people who were left behind. And in the process of all these calls to surrender, that happened from the asphalt road at 13, in the morning, most of the people who were on the hills decided to surrender.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ruez. Can you tell us where these people were buried, the ones who were killed in the ambushes in the general area around Bare? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as we know, these people were not buried; they were left as surface remains. There was a Norwegian team in 1996 who, under the umbrella of Ms. Elizabeth Rainer [phoen], went to this area in order to locate and start picking up these surface remains. I don't remember how many they did collect. The process, anyhow, were continued much later, and this area -- in this area the surface remains were -- I mean, I don't know if all of them were taken for sure, but some of them were found and taken by the BiH commission. But there was left there surface remains, as far as we know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You didn't answer my first question. How many witnesses were there testifying about this event? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: None of these people, as far as I know, has been called as a witness, at least not on this point, in this Tribunal. On top of my head, I would say that the spotting of these ambushes came through summary testimonies of maybe 10 people in a bunch of these few hundreds that we analysed during the summer, I mean, 10 who gave detailed and who focused on this because they experienced the events. It started with a tree that exploded. That was the start of the ambush, the signal point.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And did anybody testify in the Krstic trial?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Specifically on this aspect, I have no idea. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ruez. Now, in the Krstic trial, on page 590, on line 3, you speak about a precise period of time, and you say at noon the head of the column was cut at Konjevic Polje and the entire area blocked. Can you tell us what date that is, and describe the area on that day at precisely that hour, 12.00, because you weren't there yourself? So at 12.00 in the evening the head of the column was already passing through the intersection of Konjevic Polje, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The spear-head of the column passed Konjevic Polje during the night between the 12 and the 13. The very specific hour, I don't remind where I got it from, and I don't know if this would be 12/13 which would not be the case or 12.00 meaning midnight, so somewhere during that night.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ruez. And is what I quoted correct, from the point of view of transcript 590, line 3, you referred to 12.00 in the afternoon, at noon, and the head of the column being at Konjevic Polje?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, the head of the column probably arrived around noon, since they passed in the evening, so they probably scrambled in that place at 12.00 in the evening. I mean, again, this is more part of the fate of the front of a column, who suffered no specific problems when they crossed; rather, those who were left behind are the ones who became then the focus of investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ruez. On page 590, on lines 10 to 14, you talk about night fighting, and I quote you: "Some managed to break through during the night, but as you will later see on photographs of this area, this is open ground and it is very difficult to cross because it had been blocked by soldiers." Thank you. So my question is: Could you show us where the blocking forces were, relating to the locality in Bare where you found those bodies? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's two different areas. In the area south, General, the blocking position, that was at Konjevic Polje, where the 5th Engineer Unit is, where you have the line between Konjevic Polje and South Nova Kasaba, where the 65th Protection Regiment was. I mean, this is a different area than Bare. The problem that faced the people at 13, in the morning, who were in this area of Konjevic Polje -- east of Konjevic Polje is, indeed, having soldiers along this road made it impossible for them to try to attempt any crossing. The reason why, there was the surrender process at 13, in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Ruez, could you please clarify. On page 35, line 12, at the end, you were quoted as "... faced the people at 13, in the morning."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, after the night of 12 or the 13, once the spear-head had gone through this area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That means you were talking about the 13th day of that month and not 13 hours?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, 13 July, 13 July, in the morning, absolutely, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. I think, Mr. Tolimir, this is the appropriate time for the first break. We adjourn now for half an hour and resume quarter past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, continue, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We left off with the question -- or request from Mr. Ruez to draw the area where the blocking was, the blocking forces were. Could we please see document 651402, so -- that that's a page from that book that we mentioned earlier, so that the witness can draw or indicate on the map where that area which was blocked in Bare was.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the accused please repeat the document number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the number of that document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 65 ter 1450, page 23 of the book, the book of maps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just to clarify, this is the -- you may remember, the big book of documents and maps -- or, actually, pictures and maps that Mr. Ruez had. Yes, you've got it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We are very well prepared, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I thought he was talking about the map book. It was my problem.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So two different things, if I understand well. Again, I'm going to mark the location -- the rough location of the ambush of the 12 in the area of Bare/Kamenica, which is, in fact, an area south of Kravica. So roughly -- roughly, I would spot it in this area [marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Would you please now use a different colour pen to indicate the blocking forces and which direction they were advancing from? Could you just indicate, in a different colour and indicating with arrows, the direction of their movement?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The pen will now have a different colour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So also rough position, because this is part of a military analysis and there is another person who will come and testify about that part. But roughly the blocking position is along the road Bratunac-Konjevic Polje [marks] and going south towards Nova Kasaba.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: While we still have the map, could you tell us, was it possible to observe the sector of Bare from all those positions along the blue line that you indicated, and could they actually fire? Was there direct fire vision, as it were, from all of these positions, or did they have to use some indirect way of shooting, firing?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand your point. Again, this is a military aspect in which we didn't enter in depth. What the people say was that there were some forces in the area, indeed, who could observe and fire at them, though certainly not from the asphalt road, because the asphalt road is located behind the -- behind the hill, so impossible to see. Then the fact is that it's up to a more military person to talk about this, but once an area is spotted, artillery can shoot behind hills. But, again, this is part of the military aspect of the events in that place.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Ruez. On page 594 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could you switch on your microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I would like to tender this map into evidence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D34, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Ruez, on page 594 of your testimony in the Krstic case, lines 18 through 24, you say: "Here we will be shown some video footage which begins from the spot where the ambush was." Had we had occasion to see this video footage during your testimony on the 29th and 30th of March in this courtroom, perhaps some clarifications would not be necessary. But in this way, we would have to refer to relevant pages in the Krstic testimony. That's on page 599, lines 8 through 17, and I will read now. Could we pull it up on the screens? You said the following: "This area was processed in 1996 by a team of experts from Finland who worked there in the area in 1996, completely independent of our own activities. They collected the human remains, but it is important to mention that 600 bodies were found in this area. These were bodies of victims who had been killed in combat during -- in ambushes, during shellings, or in other -- under other circumstances that are impossible to determine in view of the information that we have, and I think that for us it is impossible to determine whether they were killed in battle or in some other way." My question for you is: Do you still maintain today what you said then?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The problem, Mr. Tolimir, we don't have this portion of the transcript on the screen, and there is some doubt if there is a page 599 in the English version. Could you clarify that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. You have before you the English version, and I read out a portion of the B/C/S version, 599, lines 8 through 17, and I quoted the relevant parts from the Krstic trial. Thank you. If he can recall, and if not, we can try and see it again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: There is no page 599, and we don't have this portion on the screen in the English version.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: It could be page 594 in the English, the last answer on the page.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I will check now why you do not have the right page, because this is in e-court because this was a transcript from the Krstic trial. I apologise. It should be page 596 and not 599. Thank you. 596 of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Lines 8 through 17.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Could the witness read this out in English and answer my question? Does he still -- would he still claim the same thing today? That's -- in English, that's pages 23 through 25 -- lines 23 through 25.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You have it in front of you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. I will just rely on, anyhow, the summary the general made. And, yes, indeed, I fully confirm what I said at that time. The only thing is that I do not have a recollection now of a precise number of surface remains that were collected by this, indeed, Finnish team. I thought I said "Norwegian" sometime ago. It was a mistake. It was, indeed, a Finnish team. Yes, indeed, they were totally independent of our work. And in addition, I have to say that the number of bodies that they have collected doesn't figure in the body count that we make, because, indeed, I confirm that these are surface remains, so we cannot know in what conditions they have died. So we consider them as war casualties, so they don't enter in a criminal case. And these bodies have been left there. There was no cleaning of the terrain. They have not been buried in any other spot. They have been left on the ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could we turn to the next page in English, please. Carry on, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Ruez, would you agree with me that I quoted your words correctly, as recorded in the transcript in the Krstic case? You said there: "It is important to stress that 600 bodies were collected here." Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. Yes, sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You also said in the next sentence: "These were the bodies of the victims who were killed in combat"?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, since we again -- since we do not prove they have been murdered, we have to consider they were killed in combat.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ruez. These 600 bodies that were collected by this Finnish team, were they the total number of those who are frequently mentioned, in the context of Srebrenica, as those who were missing?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: These people most certainly are part of those who are on the missing list of approximately 8.000 people, most probably, yes, and this is the reason why I always insist, by -- when we give figures, only talking about the people whose fate we can reconstruct and have been put in a detention centre, executed on a nearby execution field, buried in a primary grave, unburied and taken to a secondary grave. The only figure we rely on is this figure of people we can prove have been assassinated. All the others, even though we also know that during the cleaning of a terrain operation, probably some people were also executed on the spot, but these ones, we don't count them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You said, in the Krstic transcript, these were the bodies of the victims -- of people who were killed in combat, in ambush operations, or shelling operations. Do you still stand by what you said then?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, because again people on which we have any doubt on the cause of death, we will consider them as having been killed in action.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Should these people who were killed in action be on the list of those for which the accused before this Tribunal are charged, or should that number be decreased by 600? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I insist on the fact that the only number that we should use is the number of people we have determined their fate. So people that ultimately -- if you would add those found in primary mass graves and who have been left there, in addition to all those who have been exhumed from the secondary site that we can connect to these primary sites, this gives a figure. This is still not the total figure, because there are still secondary graves that we know are linked to this case and the bodies have still not yet been exhumed, so it is still not a final number. But for sure from the missing -- from a total list of the missing, those who have to be considered killed in action have to be retrieved from the total list. Yes, these are the math [Realtime transcript read in error "on maps"].

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ruez. I wanted to hear your opinion about the transcript. So these people should be removed from the total number of victims and from -- and they should not be the victims for which the accused are charged before this Tribunal. Now, could we please see 1D60, page 2 of this interview that you gave to "The Monitor." And in the B/C/S version, that's on page 3.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would just need to correct in the transcript, line 17. It's not: "Yes, they are on the maps," I said: "Yes, these are the math," mathematics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In fact, line 19.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 25 of "The Monitor," which is page 3 in e-court. Thank you. Could we now take a look at the third column, paragraph 2, where Mr. Rene's words are quoted, and you say the following, I quote: "For those victims in the woods, we have to count that they were killed in action. We know that there were clean-up operations or mop-up operations, and each group -- and every group that was taken prisoner up until after July 18th was systematically executed on the spot. For this, we have to rely only on witnesses, without any forensic findings. We -- for the most part, we believe witnesses, but if we cannot prove what they say, we do not use their testimony. That is why we consider that the large number of those deaths in the woods is actually lost for us."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So when you say it's lost for you, what, specifically, do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot certify these were my precise words, but what it means is that if we do an honest assessment of the situation, I repeat that those who we cannot prove that have been plugged in the organised extermination process, they are, in bracket, "lost for the case," since we cannot count these people as having been assassinated. This is in bracket what the expression "lost" means. They are lost for the Prosecution, let's say.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Could you tell me this, then: In the area of responsibility of the Zvornik Brigade, were there combat operations or was there any fighting between the brigade units and the column that was trying to break through towards Baljkovica and Tuzla, and did you investigate that? That's my second question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Though this is in the area of knowledge of another expert of the Prosecution, Mr. Butler, yes, I can confirm, indeed, that I have knowledge that around 15 and 16 mainly, maybe also maybe 17, there were combat operations in that area, because this is in the vicinity of a location, Nezuk, where the column crossed the lines towards Bosniak-Muslim-held territory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Judge Mindua has a question for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, indeed, I have a question on this matter. The bodies of people who were -- who died during military operations, during combat, and persons who would have been killed later on, my question is this: Do you have any form of certainty concerning the fact that during the burial in graves, in the first primary ones and then in the secondary ones, wasn't there also -- weren't there also some bodies of combat operations which would also have been buried there? Combat remains, I think, is -- are you absolutely certain that only the people who were killed after combat were buried in the primary and secondary graves?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When you look at the dates of the organised killing process, you can observe that it starts the 14. Burial at the first execution site starts at 13, in the evening. Burial there is finalised the 15. Then the burial process goes on towards the north, continues with 16, and the final stage is after the execution the 16 at the Branjevo Farm and the Pilica Dom, where the exhumation work is finalised with 17. So, indeed, as all this happens as even the Zvornik Brigade commander says and wrote, that he had to deal with two situations at once, one is combat operation, second is dealing with all these prisoners. It would be extremely hard to imagine that at the same time the Bosnian Serb Army is confronting this column, they also go on the battle-field to collect dead enemy soldiers and then ship them to these execution sites. As an example, very close to the Orahovac site there is a little path going towards some fields, and approximately at 150 metres away from the execution site, when we arrived there, there was a dead body. In fact, there was a skeleton. And this skeleton, though it was very close to the initial burial site, has not been picked up, and the local farmer drove on these bones probably twice a day. So my assumption is that no dead body was collected in that vicinity to be put in the graves during the material time-frame, that makes it extremely difficult to think that it happened. And in relation to that, I think that the records of the Engineering Unit of the Zvornik Brigade, there is absolutely no record of collecting bodies in this area away from the execution sites. I hope my answer is clear enough. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, absolutely, your answer is very clear. We're just waiting for the end of the translation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Now Judge Nyambe has a question for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Right. I just need some clarification. I think it's page 45. In your response to Judge Mindua, you say: "And this skeleton, although it was very close to the initial burial site, has not been picked up, and the local farmer drove on these bones probably twice a day." You say that as a fact or you are presuming that this happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We found this body when we did the first survey of this area. That was in April 1996. With a little team who was present with me was Professor [indiscernible], a pathologist, and he's the one who looked at these bones who, indeed, were -- I mean, I think we have a photograph of that, but who was lying on this path, and you had the traces of a little vehicle who was probably going back and forth along this little path to go to some field, and no one ever even thought picking up these bones and pushing them aside, even without talking about burial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Then how do you link what you have just said with the continuation of your statement: "... so my assumption is that the dead body was collected in that vicinity to be put in the graves during the material time-frame"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I said exactly the opposite. I said that my assumption is that no dead body was collected in this area to be put in this grave where only those who have been executed on the spot have been buried.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Okay, thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Ruez, the victims from the combat in the area of responsibility of the Zvornik Brigade, do you count them as those killed, the ones that you found in primary and secondary graves, or do you subtract them from the total number of killed because they were killed in combat? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Definitely, yes. Again and again, I can only repeat that the figure that we can take into consideration to have the assessment of a total number of people who went through this organised killing process are the ones that we can make the addition from grave after grave.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
